This study introduces a novel Poisson autoregressive model designed to capture time-varying characteristics in count data. The model incorporates a time-varying coefficient for the autoregressive component and a time-varying variance for the error term, both modeled through a linear combination of past observations. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the model's solution and propose a recursive least squares estimation method. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed estimator performs effectively. Furthermore, the model's utility is illustrated using daily data on the number of tweets related to the term "bitcoin" from Twitter. The findings indicate that the volatility of tweet counts exhibits significant time-varying behavior, which can be effectively captured by the proposed model. Additionally, the results suggest that the volatility of tweet counts is influenced by the volume of tweets from the preceding day. The proposed model offers a valuable tool for analyzing the temporal dynamics of count data volatility. The source code for this model is available at https://github.com/ChengCheng1992/TVPAR.

This study introduces a new method for measuring atmospheric aerosol optical depth (AOD) by leveraging the photometric variability of stars. The approach relies on the fact that stars exhibit apparent variability due to interstellar and atmospheric extinction, which can be corrected using stellar photometry. We developed a technique to quantify this variability and derived a corresponding AOD value. The method was validated using data from the ZodiCam instrument at the 1.5-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). Results indicate that the new method yields AOD values comparable to those from the standard star-based technique, with a mean difference of 0.003 ± 0.004. Furthermore, the new method offers a significant advantage: it does not require variable stars, which are scarce and difficult to identify. Instead, it utilizes the variability caused by atmospheric and interstellar extinction, which is more prevalent. This enables the use of a larger number of stars for AOD determination, thereby reducing uncertainties. Additionally, the method can be applied to any star within the field of view, allowing for the creation of spatially resolved AOD maps. These maps could enhance the accuracy of photometric corrections for exoplanet surveys. The method is detailed in Section 2, with results and conclusions presented in Sections 3 and 4, respectively.

Monte Carlo methods, particularly Metropolis-Hastings algorithms, have long been the standard for sampling configurational distributions in molecular systems. However, these approaches often suffer from poor sampling efficiency due to the high rejection rates inherent in local search strategies. In contrast, Langevin dynamics offers a stochastic alternative that enables more effective configurational sampling. This study introduces a novel implementation of Langevin dynamics designed to be both robust and efficient. We introduce a new integrator that ensures energy conservation and stability, and we propose a modified acceptance criterion that enhances sampling efficiency. Furthermore, we develop a method to dynamically adjust the integration time step, optimizing sampling performance. Our approach is validated against both Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data for a range of molecular systems, including a polymer melt, a lipid bilayer, and a protein. The results demonstrate that our method achieves a 20-fold increase in sampling efficiency compared to standard Monte Carlo techniques. Additionally, we confirm that the sampling distribution aligns with the canonical ensemble. These findings indicate that our new Langevin dynamics implementation is a powerful tool for accelerating configurational sampling in molecular systems. This study introduces a new metric for evaluating image descriptions, termed the Human Reference Utilization (HRU) score. The HRU score quantifies the extent to which an automatic description aligns with a human reference by measuring the utilization of human reference information. Unlike existing metrics, the HRU score is grounded in the concept of information utilization, which is defined by the information-theoretic measure of mutual information. We hypothesize that the HRU score will surpass current metrics in predicting human preferences for image descriptions. To test this, we conducted a large-scale preference study using 100,000 image-text pairs from the Flickr30k dataset, where 100 human annotators selected the better description between an automatic one and a human reference. The results indicate that the HRU score significantly outperforms state-of-the-art metrics in predicting human preferences. Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between the HRU score and the BLEURT metric, finding that the HRU score is a more effective predictor of human preferences than BLEURT. These findings suggest that the HRU score is a valuable tool for assessing image descriptions and could serve as a useful metric for future research in this area. This study introduces a geometric field theory of intricacy derived from the Euler-Arnold equations, which describe the dynamics of rigid body rotation. The theory is formulated on a two-dimensional spacetime manifold, where the field of intricacy is defined as the ratio of the total angular momentum to the magnitude of the instantaneous angular velocity vector. We establish that the Euler-Arnold equations constitute the equations of motion for this geometric field theory of intricacy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the conservation of total angular momentum corresponds to the conservation of intricacy, while the conservation of the angular velocity vector's magnitude aligns with the intricacy field satisfying a massless Klein-Gordon equation. Finally, we derive the energy-momentum tensor for this theory and show that the conservation of total angular momentum is equivalent to the conservation of intricacy energy. These findings suggest that the conservation of total angular momentum represents a fundamental principle in the geometric field theory of intricacy, analogous to the role of energy conservation in standard geometric field theories. Additionally, we derive the wave equation for the intricacy field and provide the corresponding general solution.

We present a forecast for the baryon-to-meson ratio in the forward rapidity region, derived from a Bayesian analysis of baryon and meson yields measured at the LHC. This prediction is grounded in a statistical hadronization model that incorporates a universal chemical freeze-out temperature and a baryon chemical potential dependent on baryon density. The model parameters were calibrated using data from Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at RHIC energies ranging from $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=7.7$ to $50.4$ GeV, as well as $p$+Pb and Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=2.76$ TeV at the LHC. The resulting forecast for the baryon-to-meson ratio in $p$+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=8.16$ TeV aligns with recent findings from the ALICE collaboration, which observed an enhancement in baryon production relative to mesons at forward rapidities. This enhancement is attributed to a baryon chemical potential that remains significant even at the low baryon densities associated with $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=8.16$ TeV. These results support the hypothesis that baryon and meson yields are governed by a universal chemical freeze-out temperature and a baryon chemical potential that varies with baryon density. Furthermore, the model successfully predicts an increase in the baryon-to-meson ratio with baryon density, a trend that could be verified in future high-energy $p$+Pb and Pb+Pb collisions at the LHC. The Bayesian framework employed here offers a valuable tool for forecasting baryon and meson yields at various collision energies, thereby aiding the design of experiments at facilities such as the FAIR and NICA colliders.

This paper introduces a framework for aligning Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) with experimental data, grounded in the $\chi^2$ minimization method. The approach involves constructing a $\chi^2$ function that incorporates the covariance matrix of the PDFs, which is derived from the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the corresponding matrix. To achieve this, we developed a method for generating the covariance matrix from the PDF's eigenvectors and eigenvalues. We validated this framework using the CT14 and NNPDF3.1 sets, confirming that the resulting $\chi^2$ values matched those reported in the original studies. Furthermore, we applied the framework to the CT14 and NNPDF3.1 sets to create new PDF sets, CT14+ and NNPDF3.1+, which were optimized to fit the specific data sets used in this work. The analysis of these new sets revealed that the $\chi^2$ values for CT14+ and NNPDF3.1+ were lower than those of CT14 and NNPDF3.1, respectively, indicating an improved fit to the data. Additionally, the uncertainties in the new sets were reduced compared to the original ones, demonstrating that the framework successfully enhanced the quality of the PDFs. This framework is applicable to any PDF set, enabling the creation of new sets tailored to specific data sets. The framework is implemented in Python and is available at https://github.com/AbdullahAlshammari/PDFAdjustment.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is primarily designed to investigate the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a state of matter created in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. However, the LHC also offers a unique environment for studying small systems, such as proton-proton (pp) and proton-nucleus (pA) collisions. These systems are too small to form a QGP, yet they exhibit collective behavior similar to that observed in larger systems. This review examines the collective phenomena found in small systems at the LHC, focusing on the emergence of anisotropic flow and the suppression of high transverse momentum particles. We also discuss the potential origins of these effects, including initial state correlations, final state interactions, and hydrodynamic behavior. Finally, we outline the remaining open questions regarding collective effects in small systems. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique for accelerating cryptographic operations on CPUs by intentionally reducing CPU frequency. Unlike existing methods that rely on specialized hardware or software, HyperDegrade leverages the CPU's native frequency scaling capabilities. The approach involves two primary components: a frequency selection algorithm that identifies the optimal frequency for each cryptographic operation, and a runtime scheduler that executes operations at their designated frequencies. We implemented HyperDegrade for RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ECDH using OpenSSL 1.1.1, and for AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, and XChaCha20-Poly1305 using BoringSSL. Our implementation of HyperDegrade outperforms OpenSSL 1.1.1 by 1.1x to 1.3x and BoringSSL by 1.1x to 1.2x across various cryptographic algorithms and key sizes. Furthermore, HyperDegrade surpasses the performance of OpenSSL 1.1.1 and BoringSSL even when those systems run on CPUs with higher frequencies. These results demonstrate that HyperDegrade can enhance cryptographic operation speeds on CPUs with lower frequencies, making it particularly beneficial for IoT devices and other resource-constrained systems. This study introduces a tactical framework for multi-agent collaboration among conventional networked robots operating under limited computational and communication resources. The proposed approach utilizes a hierarchical architecture where a high-level planner generates a global strategy, which is then executed by a low-level controller. To address the challenge of global state estimation, the paper presents a novel algorithm that leverages a distributed Kalman filter to create a local state estimator. Furthermore, a new method for optimizing the global strategy is detailed, which incorporates a heuristic to manage the extensive search space inherent in tactical problems. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through a simulated urban air defense scenario. Results indicate that the algorithm can generate a global strategy within a 100-second timeframe for a battlefield measuring 100 by 100 kilometers, involving 100 enemy aircraft and 100 friendly UAVs. Additionally, the framework's performance is validated under various communication and computational constraints. These findings suggest that the approach is viable for real-world tactical applications involving conventional networked robots with restricted capabilities. The detection of gravitational waves relies on laser interferometers, which function by measuring minute variations in the arm lengths of an L-shaped configuration. These variations arise from the passage of gravitational waves and manifest as interference patterns in the light beams. However, the sensitivity of these interferometers diminishes at high frequencies due to the finite speed of light, a limitation that hinders the identification of signals from binary neutron star mergers. To address this, we introduce a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a novel design that enhances sensitivity at high frequencies. We demonstrate that this new configuration can achieve a sensitivity improvement of up to a factor of 100 at 10 kHz compared to conventional interferometers. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid system that combines a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer with a standard one to create a broadband detector with superior overall sensitivity. This hybrid approach could enable the observation of gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers at distances approximately 20% greater than those detectable by current interferometers. Detailed descriptions of the sloshing-Sagnac and hybrid configurations, along with their associated sensitivities, are provided. Additionally, we outline the necessary modifications to convert existing interferometers into sloshing-Sagnac or hybrid systems and discuss the potential for implementing this upgrade in current detectors. Finally, we examine the impact of seismic and thermal noise on the sensitivity of the sloshing-Sagnac and hybrid configurations.

Although neural language models have largely superseded $n$-gram models in recent years, the latter remain popular due to their simplicity, transparency, and low computational requirements. In this study, we introduce a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both $n$-gram and neural models. Our method utilizes a neural network to learn a residual function, which is added to the output of an $n$-gram model to generate the final prediction. We demonstrate that this approach achieves superior performance compared to standard neural models. Furthermore, we show that incorporating a 4-gram linguistic model into the residual learning framework yields better results than using a 3-gram model. Finally, we apply this method to the task of neural text creation, where the model learns to generate text from a given source. Our findings indicate that the hybrid model outperforms both the baseline $n$-gram model and the standard neural model. Additionally, the hybrid model surpasses the baseline in terms of perplexity, BLEU score, and human evaluation metrics. These results suggest that integrating a 4-gram linguistic model into the residual learning framework enhances the quality of generated text. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to incorporate a 4-gram linguistic model into a neural text creation framework. Our approach offers a simple yet effective solution for improving neural text creation, and we anticipate that this method will be valuable for future research in this area. Accurate vote tallies are essential for ensuring fair elections. While manual counting is prone to human error, automated systems like Tesseract and CRNN have been adopted by election officials to assist with ballot processing. However, these models were trained on general text datasets and may not perform optimally on the specific layout of election ballots. This paper introduces iOCR, an informed OCR system designed to enhance accuracy for vote counting. By leveraging the known structure of ballots, iOCR employs a two-stage approach: first, it uses a layout model to predict the correct answer for each field, and second, it applies an OCR model to generate a candidate answer, which is then compared against the layout prediction. If the OCR output matches the predicted answer, it is accepted; otherwise, the system defaults to the layout prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating the layout model with Tesseract and CRNN significantly improves accuracy. Specifically, the system achieves 99.9% accuracy with Tesseract and 99.8% with CRNN on the 2020 Wisconsin ballot dataset, surpassing the performance of both standalone OCR models and the layout model alone. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/PranavBhargavi/iOCR.

This study examines the atmospheric circulation patterns of terrestrial and giant planets using simplified global circulation models (GCMs). The model incorporates a simplified radiative-convective equilibrium scheme and a shallow convection parameterization, with the vertical resolution determined by the number of atmospheric layers. We find that the circulation structure is primarily governed by the Rossby number ($Ro$), which represents the ratio of inertial to Coriolis forces, and the Reynolds number ($Re$), which balances inertial and viscous forces. For high $Ro$ values, the atmosphere exhibits a super-rotating jet at the equator, with the jet's width increasing as $Ro$ rises. In contrast, low $Ro$ conditions result in a barotropic, zonal, turbulent flow. The transition from super-rotation to turbulence occurs at a critical $Ro$ value of approximately 0.1, aligning with the $Ro$ ranges observed on terrestrial and giant planets. Additionally, the zonal wind speed scales with the planetary rotation rate ($\Omega$) and the Rossby deformation radius ($L_D$) according to the relationship $U \sim \Omega L_D$. This scaling holds true for both the super-rotating and turbulent regimes. These results suggest that the circulation structures of terrestrial and giant planets are largely driven by the planetary rotation rate and atmospheric viscosity, with the Coriolis force playing a dominant role in shaping the circulation patterns. These findings offer insights into the atmospheric dynamics of terrestrial and giant planets and could aid in interpreting the circulation patterns of exoplanets. This paper introduces the Instructor-Pupil framework, a novel approach to knowledge acquisition in first-order logic (FOL) designed to enhance the reasoning capabilities of existing systems. The framework operates through two distinct phases: an instruction phase, where an instructor provides examples of FOL sentences and their corresponding truth values, and a learning phase, where a pupil system derives a knowledge base (KB) from these examples. The resulting KB is then utilized to evaluate new sentences. We present a survey of current knowledge acquisition methods, focusing on those that employ logical entailment to derive the KB. Furthermore, we detail the Instructor-Pupil framework, which leverages a neural network to generate the KB. We also describe a hybrid method that combines the neural approach with traditional logical entailment-based techniques. Finally, we report on an evaluation of these methods conducted using the OpenBookQA dataset. The findings indicate that the neural-based approach outperforms the logical-based method, while the hybrid approach surpasses both. Additionally, we introduce a new metric for assessing knowledge acquisition methods and demonstrate that the neural-based method achieves higher scores on this metric compared to the logical-based one. Automated evaluation of natural language generation systems has become essential for large-scale applications, yet existing metrics often lack the precision required for rigorous analysis. This study investigates the dependence of the triangular flow, $v_3$, on transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) and centrality in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=200$ GeV. The analysis utilizes a multiphase transport model (AMPT) that incorporates parton and hadron cascade mechanisms. The results indicate that the $v_3(p_{\mathrm{T}})$ values from the AMPT model align well with experimental data from the STAR collaboration. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the initial spatial anisotropy, quantified by the eccentricity $\epsilon_3$, is the primary driver of the anisotropic flow $v_3$. Additionally, the study finds that the $v_3(p_{\mathrm{T}})$ in Au+Au collisions is more sensitive to the hadronic cascade mechanism than in Cu+Cu collisions. Finally, the $v_3(p_{\mathrm{T}})$ in both systems exhibits a dependence on the parton cascade mechanism, which is linked to the initial anisotropy. These findings suggest that both parton and hadron cascade mechanisms play significant roles in generating anisotropic flow in heavy ion collisions. The results also imply that the sensitivity of $v_3(p_{\mathrm{T}})$ to the parton cascade mechanism increases with the initial anisotropy. Consequently, smaller collision systems, such as p+Pb and Au+Au, may offer greater sensitivity to the parton cascade mechanism than larger systems like Cu+Cu. Ultimately, the $v_3(p_{\mathrm{T}})$ in Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions serves as a valuable probe for exploring the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma. The data presented here were collected by the STAR collaboration at BNL.

We investigate the connection between the spin distribution of massive black holes in active galactic nuclei and the existence of ultralight bosons. This study addresses the bias inherent in the line-of-sight (LOS) component of vector magnetic fields, which is a derived quantity. We demonstrate that this bias arises from the non-linear relationship between the LOS component and the Stokes parameters. Consequently, the bias in the derived LOS component is influenced by the bias in the measured Stokes parameters. We validate this correction approach using both simulated data and observations from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Our findings indicate that the bias in the measured Stokes parameters from the HMI is primarily caused by the non-linear response of the Inverse Filter (IF) to the intensity. Therefore, we suggest that the bias in the derived LOS component from the HMI is mainly due to the non-linear response of the IF to the intensity. To further reduce this bias, we propose a method to correct the bias in the measured Stokes parameters by accounting for the non-linear response of the IF to the intensity. Finally, we confirm that correcting the bias in the measured Stokes parameters effectively reduces the bias in the derived LOS component. These results suggest that the bias in the derived LOS component originates from the non-linear response of the IF to the intensity. To alleviate this bias, it is necessary to correct the bias in the measured Stokes parameters by considering the non-linear response of the IF to the intensity. This work provides a framework for reducing bias in derived measurements, which can be applied to other solar vector magnetic field instruments. This paper introduces the concept of timelike Bertrand curves within a semi-Riemannian manifold of dimension $n \geq 3$, where the metric has signature $(1, n-1)$. The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted by $\beta(G)$, represents the minimum cardinality of a resolving set for $G$. In this work, we introduce the concept of the shortened metric dimension, defined as the smallest cardinality of a resolving set $S$ such that the subgraph induced by $S$ contains no isolated vertices. We establish that for any tree $T$ with at least three leaves, the shortened metric dimension is exactly one less than the standard metric dimension. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound for the shortened metric dimension of arbitrary graphs and characterize the graphs that achieve this bound. Finally, we examine the relationship between the metric dimension and the shortened metric dimension for specific graph classes, including cycles, complete graphs, and complete bipartite graphs. These findings are significant for applications in sensor networks, where sensor nodes must be strategically placed to uniquely identify the locations of other nodes within a graph. The shortened metric dimension offers a practical measure of the minimum number of sensors required to ensure that no two sensors share the same location. This constraint is particularly relevant in scenarios where sensor nodes are deployed along the edges of a graph, such as in sensor networks designed to monitor the perimeter of a building.

While the mechanisms driving this mass-dependent evolution remain unclear, the connection between specific star formation rate ($\rm sSFR$) and mass ($M_*$) exhibits a turnover at $M_*\sim10^{10.5-11}\,\rm M_\odot$, coinciding with the emergence of bulges. The proliferation of fake news, particularly through social media, poses a significant threat to public safety and democratic processes. While deep learning models have been effective at identifying counterfeit news, they require extensive training on large volumes of data. This paper introduces a geometric approach to verifying the correctness of programs, termed the geometric principle. This principle enables the derivation of a novel, automated method for testing programs against a suite of cases. The core idea involves representing the correctness of a program as a geometric object, specifically a commutative diagram. This work offers a concise proof of the existence of clear Serre weights for $\mathrm{GL}_2$ over imaginary quadratic fields, utilizing Kummer theory. The demonstration relies on the fact that the Galois group of the maximal abelian extension of an imaginary quadratic field $K$ with exponent $p^n$ is isomorphic to the direct product of two copies of the group of units in the ring of integers of $K[p^n]$. This result is significant for the study of potential weight multiplicities in Serre's conjecture and its generalizations. The proof is elementary and does not require the use of class field theory. Additionally, this paper serves as a self-contained, elementary introduction to Serre weights, their definition, and their relevance to Serre's conjecture. The findings are applicable to the investigation of potential weight multiplicities in the generalized Serre conjecture proposed by Gee, Paškūnas, and Roberts. This study introduces a novel iterative matrix inversion method that leverages higher-order techniques to accelerate the process. The approach combines a standard iterative algorithm with an advanced order method, which itself integrates a low-order iteration with a high-order correction. We present a generalized formulation of this advanced order technique, termed the Generalized Advanced Order (GAO) method, and demonstrate that it can be implemented with a computational complexity of $O(n^{2.5})$. Furthermore, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called the Generalized Iterative Higher-Order (GIHO) method, which incorporates the GAO technique. The GIHO algorithm achieves a complexity of $O(n^{\log_2(3)})$, representing a significant improvement over the conventional iterative method's $O(n^2)$ complexity. We validate the efficacy of the GIHO algorithm through numerical experiments, showing that it surpasses both the standard iterative approach and the GAO method in terms of speed. Additionally, we confirm that the GIHO algorithm is suitable for GPU acceleration. Finally, we provide a generalized formulation of the GIHO algorithm, which can be adapted to any matrix size. These findings suggest that the GIHO algorithm is a viable candidate for real-time applications involving large-scale matrix inversions. Situational linear bandits represent a significant extension of the standard linear bandit framework, where the context space is structured as a graph. In this model, the agent's objective is to maximize cumulative rewards by selecting actions for specific situations, which are defined as pairs of a node and an edge within the graph. This work introduces a novel, fully distributed algorithm designed for a network of agents operating on a situational linear bandit problem. The algorithm requires no prior knowledge of the graph's structure and operates without any communication between agents. We establish a lower bound for the cumulative regret in this setting and demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves a matching upper bound. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to address the situational linear bandit problem in a fully distributed environment where the graph structure remains unknown. We investigate how dust growth influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our findings indicate that dust settling and coagulation can trigger a hydrodynamic instability in the disk's midplane, which we term the dust-driven instability (DDI). This instability arises because dust settling and coagulation reduce the gas-to-dust opacity, thereby increasing the gas temperature gradient and driving an instability similar to the thermal gravitational instability. The DDI operates at lower wavenumbers than the VSI, with its growth rate peaking at approximately 0.001 times the local Keplerian frequency. This rate is comparable to that of the VSI in dust-free environments. However, the DDI's growth rate is highly sensitive to the dust size distribution; it increases with larger dust sizes up to a point, after which it declines due to dust settling. In disks with a power-law size distribution, the DDI growth rate is maximized when the largest dust size is around 100 $\mu$m. We conclude that the DDI can significantly affect the evolution of dust size distributions in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Furthermore, the coexistence of the VSI and DDI may lead to complex dust dynamics in these areas. These results suggest that dust growth and the associated reduction in opacity can drive instabilities in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, potentially accelerating dust settling and coagulation. Consequently, the VSI and DDI could play crucial roles in the formation of giant planet cores in these regions. Our study highlights the importance of including dust growth in hydrodynamic simulations of protoplanetary disks. Additionally, the DDI may help explain the rapid dust settling and growth observed in the outer regions of the TW Hya disk, as reported by \cite{2016ApJ...825..113A}. Finally, the DDI could contribute to the development of dust clumps in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks.

Federated learning (FL) enables the training of deep neural networks across distributed data sources without requiring data centralization. However, existing FL methods often fail to achieve optimal performance when dealing with data drawn from diverse distributions. This study introduces a novel approach called Random Stroll for Education (RSE), which leverages the concept of random walks to enhance the efficacy of FL under diverse data distributions. The core idea involves periodically selecting a subset of data from a specific source to undergo additional training, thereby creating a specialized model for that source. This model is then shared with other data sources to improve their model performance. We demonstrate that RSE outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in scenarios involving diverse data distributions. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis showing that RSE achieves a faster convergence rate than traditional FL methods. Experimental results confirm that RSE surpasses conventional FL approaches in both convergence speed and final accuracy. We demonstrate that single-particle entanglement can produce genuine nonlocal phenomena, such as the nonlocal guidance effect responsible for nonlocal interference. This effect arises from the nonlocal nature of the entangled wavefunction, which guides the particle's nonlocal trajectory. Consequently, the nonlocality of single-particle entanglement is a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics, not merely a consequence of many-particle entanglement. This finding implies that the nonlocality of many-particle entanglement is also a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, rather than an emergent property resulting from single-particle entanglement. These conclusions are derived from a nonlocal hidden variable theory that incorporates single-particle entanglement, which we term the nonlocal single-particle entanglement theory. This theory aligns with all experimental results and offers a novel perspective on the nonlocality of quantum mechanics. We also introduce a new nonlocal single-particle entanglement experiment that could serve as a decisive test to distinguish between quantum mechanics and this alternative theory. Ultimately, we argue that the nonlocality of single-particle entanglement is a fundamental characteristic of quantum mechanics, and that the nonlocality of many-particle entanglement is likewise fundamental, not emergent. These insights provide a fresh understanding of quantum nonlocality. The proposed nonlocal single-particle entanglement experiment is feasible and could be implemented in the near future.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are widely adopted for video identification tasks due to their powerful feature extraction capabilities. However, their high computational complexity and memory requirements create significant challenges for deployment on resource-constrained devices. However, their practical application has been hindered by the high computational costs associated with estimating marginal likelihoods. We demonstrate that combining multiple methods yields optimal results, with the specific combination depending on the complexity of the models under consideration. Our findings indicate that a simple model incorporating only CMB data offers the best fit for the combined CMB and LSS dataset. Discourse markers, such as "however" and "therefore," are essential for conveying the relationships between sentences and paragraphs. While numerous studies have investigated the semantic roles of these markers, there has been limited success in creating a comprehensive taxonomy that covers all discourse indicators and their associated functions. This paper introduces a novel approach to automatically analyzing the semantic functions of discourse indicators. We developed a dataset called DiscSense, which includes 10,000 English sentence pairs annotated with the specific function of the discourse indicator connecting them. Our findings indicate that existing neural models for sentence pair classification, which rely on end-to-end training, struggle to accurately identify the functions of discourse indicators. To address this, we propose a new architecture that incorporates a contextualized lexicon-based representation of discourse indicators. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed architecture significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we conducted a detailed analysis of the distribution of discourse indicators and their functions within the DiscSense dataset. The dataset, code, and models are available at https://github.com/linguamatics/DiscSense.

We introduce a novel neural network architecture, termed the speed field network (SFN), designed to reconstruct the dark matter (DM) mass distribution from the cosmic speed field (CSF). This approach represents a significant advancement over existing methods, which rely on the halo mass function (HMF) to infer DM mass distribution. By leveraging the CSF, our method offers a more direct and accurate reconstruction of the DM mass distribution. We trained the SFN using a combination of N-body simulations and neural emulators. The results indicate that the SFN can accurately recover the DM mass distribution across a wide range of scales, from $0.1$ to $100\,h^{-1}$ Mpc, with a mean relative error of $0.01$. Furthermore, the SFN surpasses the accuracy of traditional methods, such as the HMF-based approach, in reconstructing the DM mass distribution. These findings suggest that the CSF is a valuable observable for investigating the DM mass distribution and its associated physical processes. Additionally, the SFN architecture can be adapted to reconstruct other physical quantities from various cosmological observables. This study employs a relativistic initial principles framework to investigate the electronic structure of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states arising from magnetic adatoms and dimers on a metallic surface. The analysis utilizes a relativistic tight-binding model to construct the surface's electronic band structure, which is subsequently folded into a reduced zone. This approach enables the determination of the electronic structure for a specific Mn adatom and two distinct configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. The resulting band structures reveal the formation of YSR states, which manifest as sharp peaks within the superconducting gap of Nb. These findings align with previous initial principles calculations and experimental observations. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of spin-orbit coupling and the magnetic moment on the YSR states. The results indicate that spin-orbit coupling significantly alters the band structure, whereas variations in the magnetic moment have a negligible effect. Additionally, the analysis of the local density of states (LDOS) demonstrates that the YSR states are predominantly localized around the Mn adatom and dimer sites. Finally, the study explores the impact of the Mn adatom's and dimers' magnetic moments on the supercurrent flowing between them, revealing that increasing the magnetic moment reduces the supercurrent. These results suggest that the supercurrent between the Mn adatom and dimers is highly sensitive to their magnetic moments. Overall, this work provides a relativistic initial principles framework for investigating YSR states in magnetic adatoms and dimers on metallic surfaces, offering valuable insights into the electronic structure of such systems. The proposed framework is applicable to various magnetic adatoms and dimers on metallic surfaces. Early detection is crucial for effective treatment, yet manual diagnosis by medical professionals is often time-consuming and prone to errors. This study introduces a novel framework that combines a ResNet50-based deep learning model with an outlier detection method to identify and remove anomalous samples from the dataset. The proposed approach utilizes a ResNet50 architecture to classify skin images into five categories: melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis, and benign lesions. By integrating an outlier detection mechanism, the system identifies and excludes abnormal data points, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves an accuracy of 99.98%, a precision of 99.98%, a recall of 99.98%, and an F1 score of 99.98%. These findings indicate that the hybrid framework of ResNet50 and outlier detection significantly improves classification performance. Muon-neutrino interactions represent a significant source of background in future high-energy muon colliders. These events are characterized by the emission of a forward-going, highly energetic vector boson, which subsequently decays into a lepton pair. This process, known as lepton-number-tagging, is essential for identifying muon neutrino interactions. However, the associated efficiency loss poses a major challenge for the event selection required at muon colliders. To address this, we introduce a fast, accurate method for estimating vector boson emission in neutrino interactions, termed VEST. This technique leverages a neural network trained on Monte Carlo simulations to predict the vector boson's transverse momentum. We validate the accuracy of VEST by comparing its predictions against a standard Monte Carlo estimator. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating VEST into a selection strategy yields a 10% improvement in efficiency compared to conventional methods. Finally, we confirm that VEST maintains high accuracy even when applied to Monte Carlo samples generated with a different event generator. These findings indicate that VEST can serve as a reliable estimator for vector boson emission in neutrino interactions at high-energy muon colliders. Invariant sets, particularly invariant curves and surfaces, play a crucial role in comprehending the global dynamics of differential equations. This paper introduces a novel approach to identify invariant surfaces in systems of differential equations. We demonstrate that the existence of such surfaces is contingent upon the integrability of a specific first-order partial differential equation. Leveraging this finding, we establish that fractional-order systems with a sum of orders exceeding two cannot possess invariant surfaces. Consequently, chaotic attractors in these systems must arise from the interaction of at least two invariant curves. We conclude by outlining the necessary conditions for the existence of invariant curves in fractional-order systems. These results are significant for both theoretical investigations and practical applications of fractional-order dynamical systems. Furthermore, our method for detecting invariant surfaces offers a valuable tool for analyzing the global dynamics of differential equations. This study addresses the inverse challenge of a structural acoustic interaction between a cantilever beam and a spherical projectile. The beam's response is captured using a laser vibrometer, while the projectile's trajectory is tracked via a high-speed camera. The objective is to reconstruct the projectile's impact point and velocity from the recorded data. To achieve this, a finite element model of the beam is developed and validated against experimental results. An optimization algorithm is then employed to determine the impact location and velocity that best align the model's output with the measured data. The findings indicate that the reconstruction accuracy is highly sensitive to the beam's initial conditions, particularly its initial velocity. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of combining finite element models with optimization algorithms to reconstruct impact details from structural acoustic data, offering a viable approach for forensic investigations into structural damage. We introduce the minimal extension of the simplest scoto-seesaw model capable of generating a sub-eV neutrino mass via the seesaw mechanism. This framework incorporates a single complex scalar singlet, which serves as the dark matter candidate. We examine the model's parameter space, focusing on neutrino oscillation data, direct dark matter detection limits, and electroweak precision constraints. Our analysis reveals that dark matter detection experiments impose the most stringent constraints, while neutrino oscillation data and electroweak precision requirements are easily satisfied. We find that the dark matter mass is bounded between 10 and 100 GeV, with the neutrinoless double beta decay rate remaining below current experimental limits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the scalar sector vacuum is stable and robust against thermal corrections. Finally, we identify a region of parameter space where the dark matter annihilation cross-section aligns with the thermal freeze-out mechanism, offering a viable solution to the cosmic dark matter abundance. This region is characterized by a dark matter mass near 40 GeV and a singlet vacuum expectation value around 10 GeV. Consequently, this represents the minimal scoto-seesaw framework where dark matter achieves the correct relic abundance through freeze-out, a scenario that has been extensively studied in other models but not yet in the simplest scoto-seesaw variant. We anticipate that this model will be testable at future dark matter detection experiments and colliders.
